content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the design now—whether a prop group needs a root joint at all, since plain objects without joints might just default to parts anchored at the root with no explicit position, unlike the lid which needs its own joint for movement.

I'll create a single root joint at the origin plus a hinge joint for the chest lid. For the overall composition, I'm envisioning a League of Legends-style treasure hoard: an open chest with a hinged lid, a mound of overflowing coins, glowing faceted gems, a spiky jeweled crown, flared goblets, maybe a sword, urn, and scepter, all sitting on a roughly 1.6m rug or stone base. The chest itself would be about 0.9m wide with an exaggerated barrel-vault lid, oversized gold bands, spiked corner brackets, and a glowing cyan-magenta arcane lock as the centerpiece detail.

I'm thinking through the color palette and surface treatment -- deep indigo wood contrasted against saturated gold, with magenta and cyan gem accents, using hand-painted gradient textures to mimic a splash-art look, including wood grain and noise-based countershading on the gold.

For the coins, I'm working out an efficient way to represent hundreds of them: simple 8-sided cylinder coins (~24 tris each) merged by color group (gold, light gold, silver) to keep the triangle budget reasonable at scale, then building the overall mound as a squashed, scale-textured lump with individual coins scattered on top for a believable silhouette.

For gems, I'm considering faceted geometries (octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron) with flat shading in ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, and topaz tones, and weighing whether emissive glow would wash out the facet shading -- leaning toward keeping most gems unglowing with saturated colors so lighting preserves the facets, while reserving glow for just a few standout crystals.

I'm also planning magical light effects like glowing rays spilling from an open chest, implemented as soft billboard cards with alpha cutouts rather than real transparency.

I'm picturing extra flourishes too: floating four-point star sparkles above the hoard, and a stone dais beneath everything with a glowing cyan rune ring to anchor the top-down composition.

Now I'm sizing the dais at about 0.95m radius and 0.08m tall, making sure the lowest model points touch the floor while floating sparkles and light rays stay within a reasonable height ceiling. I'm mapping out the top-down layout starting with the chest positioned near center with an open, tilted lid.

For the lid, I'm shaping it as an extruded arc profile to create a vaulted dome form, then rotating it roughly -105° about the hinge at the back top edge to depict it swung open.

So -110° makes the lid stand up and lean back slightly past vertical, and I'm checking how the dome's bulge orients once rotated into that open position.

The cleanest approach is to build all lid parts assigned to the hinge/lid bone so they inherit the pose transform automatically, rather than trying to compute rotated coordinates manually for each piece—I'll make a helper function that tags parts with the lid bone by default.

For the chest interior, I'm planning a walled box lined with velvet, filled to the rim with a mound of gold coins spilling over the front edge onto the dais, using a squashed faceted icosphere for the coin heap plus scattered loose coins, and flanking goblets near the front corners.

Now adding more treasure props: three distinct goblets (a tall ruby chalice, a wide sapphire cup, and one tipped over spilling coins), a bulging burlap sack with a tied neck leaking coins, and smaller accent pieces like a draped pearl necklace, a fallen scepter, and a ring scattered around the chest base.

The crown becomes the centerpiece, perched atop the front mound slightly right of center — a tall exaggerated design with five curvy spiked points tipped in glowing gems, built from a closed circular band with radial spike extrusions rather than any tilted transform, sitting upright on a flattened part of the mound.

For the overall budget I'm targeting roughly 450-600 parts and under 60k triangles. For color, I'm leaning into League of Legends' saturated high-contrast style: deep indigo-teal shadows, gold as the dominant hue, and a magical cyan glow as accent.

For the chest itself, I'm considering a Hextech-adjacent but original take: lacquered deep teal-navy wood with gold bands and a cyan rune-glow lock, playing cool chest tones against warm gold hoard contents. The dais would be dark slate-purple stone etched with cyan runes, the crown gold with magenta gems and a central cyan gem, and goblets in gold, silver, and rose gold for variety. For the wood texture I'm planning a grain pattern running along the main axis using a darker base with lighter streaks.

Writing paint functions...

Still writing coin and dais paint code...

Adding a glowing cyan rune ring decal with concentric circles, tick marks, simple glyph shapes, and an eight-pointed star, sized for a plane texture, while figuring out proper orientation for the plane geometry.

Now I'm positioning the decal just above the dais lathe top to avoid z-fighting, and designing stylized golden light rays as tapered kite-like spikes radiating outward from the chest, using gradient alpha cuts for sharp edges.

Still working out the ray card geometry...

Using cross:true for rays so they read from the top-down camera too, since the rays shoot up and slightly forward from the open chest. For sparkles I'll scatter small 4-point star glyphs with glow randomly across the hoard, varying sizes roughly between 0.05 and 0.12.

I'm also considering a few floating gems hovering above the chest for extra flair, though they add height and aren't physically attached, so I'll keep sparkle height modest around 1.05 m and note the floating pieces as loose, unconnected elements. For the loose gem pile itself, I want to scatter around 30 gems with varied geometric shapes like elongated octahedrons, low-detail icosahedrons, and hex-bipyramids to break up uniformity.

Designing the gem profile using a lathe shape with low segment counts (6-8) to get crisp faceted faces instead of smooth curves, with a pointed bottom, a girdle bulge, and a flat table top. I'll mix these faceted lathe gems with some emerald-cut boxes and tall hexagonal crystal clusters for variety, keeping each as its own separate part.

Now I'm adding glowing cyan and magenta crystal clusters tilted behind the chest on the dais, using a tilted lathe axis for the tall pointed crystal shapes, with three to five per side for strong color contrast and a glow strength around 0.7. I'm also laying out the chest box dimensions and positioning it as a hollow shape sitting on the dais plinth.

Working out the chest and lid geometry...

When open, the underside reads as a flat plank, so I'll add a slightly smaller velvet inset panel in plum with gold trim to make it look lined rather than bare wood. I'll keep the lid geometry low-poly, using the wood paint color with grain along x, and add thin gold arch-shaped bands across the lid as straps, built from an offset arch outline.

Positioning the gold bands at x ≈ ±0.31 with a central lock plate, plus end cap plates near x=±0.46 shaped like the arch outline with added rivets...

Now I'm planning the lid bevel and all the chest body details: gold corner angle brackets at each corner, a bottom and top rim band, a large central lock plate with a glowing cyan rune socket and keyhole, and rows of rivets merged into a single gold part separate from the lid's own rivet set. For the wood walls I'm thinking through using a painted plank texture with horizontal seam lines to simulate individual boards.

Now I'm weighing the color palette -- gold accents against a deep purple-blue or teal-blue wood tone, with cyan glow and magenta gem highlights, trying to pick a dais and chest wood shade that reads well with strong gold contrast.

For the chest interior, I'm settling on a plum-red velvet lining and planning the chest body as four walls plus a thick bottom, with a coin heap piling up near the opening to mostly obscure the inner cavity.

For the coin heap itself, I'm shaping a squashed icosahedron and deforming its vertices with a deterministic position-based function so the lumps stay seamless across duplicate vertices, then recomputing normals afterward.

I'm also adding a second lumpy pile spilling toward the front of the dais, plus a smaller mound of multicolored glowing gems off to one side, working out their positions relative to the dais radius and the chest's back placement.

I'm now working through the coordinate layout for each hoard item, and sorting out the viewer's orientation relative to the model so left and right map correctly onto the +X and -Z axes.

I'm placing the chest at the center-back and computing where its lid ends up once opened at roughly 112 degrees, tracking the hinge point and resulting height and depth.

Adjusting the lid's opening angle to 108° for a better fit. Now placing the crystal clusters behind-left and behind-right on the dais, checking their distance stays within the 1.05 radius, then positioning the crown on top of the front heap near its peak.

Next I'm scattering goblets around the chest — a standing gold goblet near the right side, a silver one tucked closer in, and a tipped goblet lying on its side with coins spilling out in front. I'm also laying out several coin stacks of varying heights around the front-right area and starting to place a sack toward the left.

I'll chain the necklace as a string of beads draping from the chest down over the hoard, with a gem pendant at the end. For extra flourishes, I'll skip scepters and scrolls but consider scattering a few jeweled rings and a crown, maybe adding simple emblem decals onto some coins for visual variety.

For the coin faces, I'm thinking of using a flat circular texture with a star emblem mapped onto the top of each coin cylinder, and trying to batch them as a single card mesh scattered across the heap using surface normals so they lie flush and face-up realistically.

I also want to scatter actual small 3D coin cylinders embedded partway into the heap surface for edge silhouette detail, each with slight random tilt and spin so they catch light individually.

To stay within budget, instead of one part per coin, I'll compute all the cylinder transforms myself from the scatter hits and merge them into a single geometry per color group, keeping it to one part per hue rather than per coin.

I'm picking five flat tones — two golds, a pale gold, a silver, and a copper — so the coins render with crisp faceted shading rather than smooth gradients, which means converting the merged geometry to non-indexed for proper flat lighting.

I need to stay under the 64 flat-color limit, budgeting roughly 8 for gems, 5 for gold, and about 15 for everything else, since painted textures don't count toward that cap. For the crown's gold band, I'm shaping it as a lathed rectangular ring profile with enough segments (16) to look smooth rather than faceted.

Now I'm designing the decorative trim—beaded rows top and bottom made from merged spheres, plus a ring of five inlaid gems oriented radially along the band. For the crown points, I'm alternating five tall prongs with curved fleur-de-lis style extrusions against five shorter arches, with gem tips on top, defining the extrude outline shape and positioning logic for each prong around the circle.

I'm also adding a red velvet inner cap as a lathe-generated dome visible inside the crown, setting up a reusable crown transform frame so lathe and extrude calls can share consistent orientation helpers, and placing a larger glowing cyan gem on the front-facing prong. Now I'm starting to sketch the goblet's lathe profile for the chalice foot and stem.

Working out the goblet bowl geometry...

The axis points are degenerate columns which is fine for the lathe. I'm thinking about adding contents to the hoard goblet—a small gold coin lump filling the bowl, plus a ring of gem studs around the base rim.

For the gem studs, I'll place small octahedron shapes in a loop, merged by color. For the tipped goblet, I'm building it upright in local space then applying a transform to tilt it so the opening faces forward and coins spill out, using a reusable local-coordinate helper class with position and quaternion that converts points and directions into world space for the lathe geometry and other shapes like the crown and sack.

I'm adding a few large floating gems above the chest with a thin glowing halo ring for a magical touch, keeping it modest so it doesn't clutter the top-down view. Then I'm tallying up the rough part counts across the chest, lid, coin heap, gems, crystals, crown, goblets, and sack to gauge overall complexity.

I'm thinking of enriching the scene with a hanging chain made from merged torus links and a small stack of gold ingots (trapezoid prisms with a stamped decal) placed near the goblets, while skipping extras like a dagger or scepter to avoid overcomplicating things. Now I'm setting up the root joint at the origin to anchor the whole hierarchy.

I'm defining the lid's hinge joint, deciding its direction and rotation axis so the pose command rotates it correctly around its own hinge position, then attaching the lid's parts to that bone before applying the pose transform once everything is built.

Everything built before the pose stays rigid to the bone, so I need to make sure non-lid parts are built directly in their final closed-position coordinates rather than being re-posed later. I'm also checking that the dais sits flush at floor level, keeping the lowest point of the model at y=0 within tolerance.

Now I'm designing the dais as a lathed profile — a stepped stone base with a bottom ring around radius 1.08 and a chamfered second ring, using roughly 16 segments so the silhouette stays round but still reads as faceted stone rather than smooth plastic, with hard creases preserved on steep angle changes.

Still shaping dais profile points...

For decoration, I'm planning a glowing rune decal just above the dais top face, sized to cover most of the platform, plus a ring of small cyan glowing studs embedded in the rim bevel to add magical accent lighting. I'm also sketching out the texture atlas budget across rune ring, coin face, sparkle, and ray textures, and starting to think through paint zones like wood and gold trim for the chest.

I'm estimating painted surface area to figure out texel density and whether a 1024 or larger atlas gives sharp enough detail for hand-painted plank textures. Writing wood plank paint function...

I'm working through the extrusion's surface coordinates, figuring out where the plank seams should fall on the arch's outer wall versus the flat faces, using the outline's u-v mapping along the thickness axis.

Now I'm planning the chest's decorative gold hardware: vertical straps on the front at x=±0.3 and a center lock plate at x=0, matching bands on the lid, plus trim boxes along the base and top rim. Time to write the code for all this.

I'm setting up helper functions for merging geometries and a collector class that groups shapes by color, flushing them into bone-attached meshes at the end. Since the cylinder geometry is indexed and the octahedron isn't, I'll convert everything to non-indexed first so merging stays consistent across position, normal, and uv attributes.

For placing gems and crown studs, I'm using matrices built from position, quaternion, and scale, computing orientation quaternions from surface normals so each piece aligns correctly to the mesh.

For the heap, I'm scattering coins and lumps across the surface, varying their tilt and burial depth so some lie flat, some tilt on edge, and some sink partially into the pile, filtering by normal direction so pieces only land on upward-facing surfaces.

For the coin emblem texture, I'm drawing a top-down coin face with a gold fill, a darker rim ring, and a star emblem using warm gold tones, applied as flat cards on the scattered hit points with a slight sink offset to avoid z-fighting with the 3D coin geometry.

Now I'm working on the gem shape, using a lathe profile to create a classic cut gem with a pointed pavilion bottom and a wider girdle, defining a function that takes size, axis, segment count, and spin to generate glowing gem meshes.

I'll scatter about 28 gems onto heap surfaces where the normal points upward enough, varying their sizes and cycling through ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, and aqua colors, lathing each at the hit point tilted along the surface normal.

I'm settling on seven flat gem colors plus a glow-material clone per strength for the crystals, then shaping the large glowing crystals as six-segment lathes with a tapered profile distinct from the gem palette.

I'm also planning dark violet rock lumps at the crystal bases for texture, plus a gold lock plate on the chest with a bevel edge, a glowing cyan hex-rune gem, and a dark keyhole socket set into the front face.

Now I'm blocking out the chest cavity as a hollow box with wall thickness 0.04, defining the floor, front, back, and side panels with their individual positions and dimensions.

I'll keep interior walls same wood with thin velvet liner slabs, then add gold rim trim bands around the top edge and a bottom gold band for detailing.

Now I'm adding corner brackets with thin box strips and cap pieces, plus small gold ball feet beneath the chest bottom for support, and placing hinge barrel cylinders on the back edge.

For the lid geometry, I'm working out the arch outline in cross-section — straight side edges rising to a curved apex — computing the arc radius from the half-chord and sagitta to define the circular shape of the lid's top profile.

Building band outlines by offsetting the arch path outward for a wrapped-band effect...

Still computing offset geometry...

Working out sweep orientation...

I'm reasoning that a polyline sweep path should work fine since the arch's corner angles are gentle enough not to trigger the rounding/splitting issues with rigid skinning, given it's a single bone. Sweeps seem like the more practical approach over extrude-with-offset for the arch band.

I'm now working out the geometry of the lid: the thick wooden arch extrudes between the side plates, the gold end-plates sit at the x-extremes, and the velvet underside panel needs its normal vector tracked through the lid's opening rotation so it faces correctly once open.

I'm placing a velvet box panel just beneath the lid's inner surface, then adding a gold border trim, decorative studs, and a small painted emblem plane (a stylized gem-star crest rendered via SVG) positioned on that underside face.

I still need to sort out the texture-facing direction once the lid rotates into its closed pose, then add a shield-shaped lock plate with a rune gem on the front body wall. I'm also working out the chest's interior heap geometry—placing an ellipsoid mass to represent contents, figuring out which part stays hidden inside versus pokes above the rim.

For the second heap piece, I'm checking how its radii and center position interact with the chest's front wall, making sure the overlapping region stays correctly tucked inside the cavity rather than clipping through the wall surface.

Then I'm placing additional smaller lumps for heap C around the sides and front of the chest, plus a scattered spill trail and a separate gem pile, working out positions and radii for each lump near the chest edges and the sack.

For coin texture I'm giving the gold a scale-like Voronoi pattern to suggest individual coins, then layering actual 3D coin cards on top. I'm also scattering roughly 60 loose coins across the dais in a front arc, tilting them slightly flat on the ground while rejecting positions that overlap the chest footprint or existing heaps.

For the burlap coin sack near the chest, I'm lathing a slumped sack profile with a tied neck and flared mouth, adding mottled burlap coloring, a red rope tie, and a gold coin emblem patch, plus a small lumpy coin pile spilling from its open top.

Nearby I'm stacking gold ingots as beveled trapezoid prisms, arranged three on the bottom, two in the middle, one on top, painted bright gold with highlights and stamped with an engraved decal plane on each top face.

Then I'm designing three goblets via a reusable lathe-based builder with gem studs and rim bands — a gold chalice with rubies, a silvery one with cyan gems, and a tipped rose-gold variant, each filled with a small heap of coins.

For the metal paints, I'm defining countershaded mottled textures for gold, silver, and rose finishes to get that hand-painted contrast look, then moving on to building a cyan rune-ring SVG with concentric strokes, tick marks, glyph shapes, and a hidden eight-point star for the hoard's magical ground decal.

I'm sizing down the texture atlas to 768px to balance the rune ring plus other elements, and scattering 24 small runic glyph marks around the ring using rotated transforms off a base shape. Now I'm moving to the coin face design — a gold circle with a bronze outer ring and a four-point star emblem — before starting on the spark element.

Still writing SVG shapes...

Then I'm sketching the lid emblem as a gold crest with a star and wings against a transparent background, followed by a darker stamped rectangle design for the ingot mark.

Setting up imports and helper utilities...

Still writing setup code...

Writing plank coloring logic...

For the dais stone I'm layering a voronoi-based flagstone texture with countershading so top faces read lighter than sides, and using the same pattern for the coin heap with a gold-brown tint.

Now I'm setting up the chest's joint hierarchy with a base root joint and a lid joint hinged at the back edge, and defaulting all parts to bone to the base unless otherwise specified.

I'm sketching the builder setup, deciding on texture atlas sizing and starting with the rune plane geometry with its glow texture mapping.

Thinking through the plane's orientation with the aim function: the front face points upward so the rune drawing reads correctly when viewed from above, and the chirality works out fine despite minor glyph asymmetry. I'm checking that the plane radius fits within the dais top surface before moving on to the coin heaps.

Now I'm writing a lump() helper that deforms an icosahedron into an irregular rounded shape using noise-based displacement scaled along each axis, then recomputes vertex normals for a faceted look. I'm working out how subdivision detail level translates into face count for the icosahedron geometry.

Since the floor is at y=0, I need to check that nothing dips below the -2% tolerance. Heap B's bottom with ry=0.2 would reach -0.1, which violates that limit, so I need to clamp the displaced vertices to stay within the allowed sink depth.

I'll implement a floor parameter that clamps local y values for each heap so the bottom never goes below the tolerance, while keeping the top at the right height. Then I'll place the heap parts and use scattering for coin placement across the heap surfaces with minimum distance constraints.

Writing coin bag code...

I'm picking a palette of gold, silver, and copper tones for the coins to keep the flat-color count low, then scattering gems separately onto the heaps with their own randomization, and positioning the cards in a pseudo-circular arrangement flattened onto the surface.

For the chest's glow, I'm deciding rays of light fanning out from the opening at a fixed center point, with angles spread between -60° and 60° and varying lengths so the center rays appear longest, each ray rendered as its own card call to control size independently.

I'm checking that the rays don't overshoot past the lid, which leans back behind the chest, and reconsidering the ray length so the overall sculpture height stays contained rather than ballooning too tall—trimming max ray length to around 0.8 so the top sits near 1.3.

Next I'm sizing the sparkle accents: small camera-facing cross-cards scattered around the chest, varying sizes and placement near the hoard's height range, which feels proportionate for the piece.

Now I'm setting up a local coordinate frame helper class to simplify positioning and orienting the crown geometry relative to its own origin and rotation.

For the crown itself, I'm defining the lathe profile for a flared gold band with slightly wider rim at the top, adding beaded trim rings along the top and bottom edges, five radial gemstone panels spaced evenly around the band with small pearls between them, and alternating tall and short prongs around the circumference with the tallest centered at the front.

Each tall prong gets a pearl-like ball gem at its tip while the shorter ones get a diamond-cut gem, and I'm adding an inner velvet dome cap sized to fit just inside the band so it peeks through the crown's open top. I'm deciding to keep the design focused on spiky prongs rather than crossing arches, aiming for a more stylized, game-like royal crown.

For positioning, I'm tilting the crown with an offset and rotation so it sits naturally sunk into the gold heap, planning to fine-tune the exact height once I preview it against the pile. I'm also placing a glowing cyan gem on the front band facing outward.

I'm now sketching a reusable goblet-building function that takes a location, metal paint, trim, gem color, scale, and whether to include coins, lathing a profile with a low segment count to get a faceted, stylized look rather than a smooth round shape.

Writing lathe profile coordinates...

Adding gem glow logic...

For the goblet's contents, I'm placing a lump of gold coins just above the rim with a heap paint style, plus a few coin cylinders, and for the tipped goblet adding a trail of spilled coins along the ground near its new position.

Now I'm working out the orientation for the tipped goblet, rotating its axis to lie horizontally on its side with the mouth tilted slightly upward toward the viewer, figuring out where the foot and bowl ends land relative to the dais surface.

Actually axis rises toward the mouth since foot radius is smaller than bowl radius, so for both to touch the floor, the foot center sits slightly higher — a gentle ~2° tilt with D.y around +0.03. I'll just iterate with preview checks to close any gap rather than solving exactly.

Now for the sack, I'm defining a faceted lathe profile with lumps and a neck flare, plus a coin bulge near the mouth, then adding a torus ring at the neck for the rope tie, laid flat by rotating it 90° on the X axis.

For applying that rotation within the local coordinate system, I'll combine it with the loc's existing quaternion using a helper method. Then I'm adding burlap-style grain texture with weave and stitch details, and a hand-placed curved necklace of beads running from the chest down into a heap.

Plotting out the necklace path with coordinates draping from the chest lip to the heap, with pearl beads placed along the curve and a pendant gem at the lowest point and a thin gold chain tube. I'll need to tune the heap heights to avoid collisions once I preview the render, then move into writing the actual structured code.

For the crystal clusters I'm designing a lathe-based prism shape with a pointed tip, flat-shaded with six segments and a glowing highlight, using a purple rock color palette for the base lumps.

I'm also planning the dais rim with glowing studs arranged in a ring, and a floating centerpiece gem with a cyan diamond shape and a tilted golden halo ring around it.

For the rays, I'll space them at angles skipping the vertical center to leave a gap near the gem. For the closure mechanism, I'm thinking of a gold hasp plate on the lid's front edge that dangles open since the lid is up, pairing with a lock plate on the body front.

Defining the lock plate shield shape...

Adding keyhole outline, corner studs, and gold corner brackets, then working out strap positions along the front face edges and reconsidering wall depth placement.

Gold paint elements use a hand-painted gradient approach applied to box geometry via position/normal data. I'm planning the chest's skirt band, top rim band, and checking for clashes with the lid when closed, then adding an interior velvet liner along the inner wall faces.

The lumpy ellipsoid coin heap needs its radius clamped so its bumps don't poke through the liner, while its dome peak stays within the cavity height. I'm also setting up coin scatter placement on the heap surface based on upward-facing normals, and starting to lay out coin stacks.

I need to position standing goblets and coin stacks across the dais so they don't overlap the heaps, checking coordinates against each heap's footprint to find clear spots.

Checking ingot and crystal placements near the chest for clearance, adjusting the crystal cluster positions slightly inward so they don't overlap the chest corners, then starting to work out where a gem pile should sit between the sack and heap B.

I'm settling on a small mound near (-0.68, 0.22) that stays clear of the sack, then laying out 3-4 coin stacks at varying heights around the upper dais area. Finally I'm planning loose coins scattered randomly across the remaining dais space, rejecting any that fall within the footprints of the chest, heaps, or other objects already placed.

I'm working out around 70 loose coins with slight tilts, keeping them thin cylinders set just above the dais surface, and defining exclusion zones (chest rectangle, heap ellipse, goblets) so nothing overlaps. I'm also sorting out the TypeScript typing for the outline points and coordinate arrays to keep the helper functions flexible.

Now I'm building the Bag class that merges geometries by color, applies transform matrices for position, rotation, and scale, then flushes each color group into a merged mesh part with optional glow and flatness settings.

Writing merge/flush logic...

Writing SVG ring code...

Still writing glyph positions...

I'm figuring out how the hoard pile occupies the center of the dais, leaving the ring and glyph band visible around the edges based on their relative radii.

Now I'm sketching a coin face design with layered gold circles, a star-shaped emblem at center, and a curved highlight arc for shine.

I'm also planning a silver variant by tinting the gold texture grey, plus spark and ray SVGs for sparkle effects, and moving on to a lid emblem design.

Still writing SVG code...

Now I'm designing a sack patch with a stitched border and a gold coin-star emblem on burlap, planning to apply it via a decal API onto the sack mesh's surface.

I'm working through the lid's hinge rotation, confirming the pose API supports axis/degree rotation, and checking that glow effects and flat-colored gems will render correctly across the lathe and painted parts, while watching for potential material compatibility issues with card meshes.

Now I'm setting up convenience wrapper functions for part creation, typing them to accept either string colors or Paint objects, and binding them to the appropriate bone (base or lid) with sensible defaults, plus a similar wrapper for lathe geometry.

Writing the dais lathe profile...

Positioning the glow studs so they sit flush against the sloped step, rotating each one around the Y-axis to align its long edge tangentially with the radius at its angle.

Now I'm defining the coin heap piles inside the chest using a lump helper that builds randomized displaced geometry, clamping vertex heights so they stay within the chest's interior walls and floor.

I'll paint the gem mound with saturated multicolor patches since it can't actually glow, then scatter around 14 real glowing gems on top for the actual sparkle. I'll use the hit scatter function across the heaps and gem pile, pulling normal and position from each hit.

Writing gem placement function...

Setting up the treasure chest structure with base and lid joints, then working out the arch geometry for the lid bands...

Computing the lid outline...

Adjusting end plate sizes...

Still mapping out the band geometry...

I'm also thinking through the lid decoration placement, since the lid leans back and its exterior dome is only partially visible from a top-down angle versus the interior, which is more visible from the front.

For the exterior I'm adding bands plus a center crest plate with a gem, while the interior underside needs a velvet panel, gold trim frame, crest decal, and studs, positioned symmetrically along x with a thin box geometry for the velvet pad and frame strips bordering it.

Now I'm working out orientation for the emblem decal plane so its "top" points toward the far edge of the lid when open, choosing the up and facing axes so the design reads correctly in world space once rotated.

I'll also add a gold lip band across the front edge of the lid for detail, proud at the opening edge.

For the lid's crest I'm placing a central gold plate with a cyan gem near the top of the arch, working out the diamond-shaped plate outline on the horizontal top plane.

Now I'm adding hinge barrels to the body as small gold cylinders rotated to lie along the X axis, positioned symmetrically at the back of the crown, before moving on to writing the actual crown detail code.

I'm defining the crown's orientation with a tilted rotation leaning toward the front-left, then lathing a ring profile with the gold color to form the crown base, adjusting the radius points to build a proper rim shape.

Now I'm adding bead trim details around the rim with rings of pearl-like spheres at top and bottom, plus an inner velvet cap using a lathed profile with a crimson-magenta color, and positioning gemstones radially around the band at 72-degree intervals embedded into the surface.

I'm assigning alternating gem colors around the ring—aqua at the front, with ruby, sapphire, and emerald variants filling the rest—then starting to build the prong geometry, alternating tall and short prongs at offset angles with lathed outlines rising from the band base.

I'm placing a gem at each prong tip, positioned along the radial and vertical axes, cycling through ruby/sapphire colors with a larger aqua gem at the front, then defining a shorter prong outline with a sharp tip for a pearl mount.

I'm deciding to skip extra details like inlaid lines, mid-prong gems, and crown arches to keep things simple, setting the pearl color to a soft white-pink. Now I'm starting to design a reusable goblet function that takes location, scale, metal, and gem parameters, building standing goblets with consistent orientation and a coin heap placed inside using the same quaternion for alignment.

I'm defining the goblet's silhouette as a profile curve, scaled by size, and checking that the outer and inner contours don't overlap or cross incorrectly to form a valid simple polygon shape.

Now I'm planning the decorative details: lathing the profile into a 3D shape with segments, then adding gold trim rings and a gem accent near the stem knot, plus a gem ring on the bowl.

I'll size the band with outer radius 0.095 and inner 0.084 for a trim ring in darker bronze, then place the gems resting on top at y=0.307. For variety, I'm considering making the second goblet a different silhouette with a non-uniform scaled bowl profile instead of a two-handled cup.
